The domain name **mil** is the sponsored top-level domain (sTLD) in the Domain Name System of the Internet for the United States Department of Defense and its subsidiary or affiliated organizations. The name is derived from _military_. It was one of the first top-level domains, created in January 1985.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/.mil#cite_note-1) As in the case with .gov, the United States is the only country that has a top-level domain for its military, a direct result of the United States' military's role in the creation of the Internet.
Other countries often use second-level domains for this purpose, e.g., _mod.uk_ for the United Kingdom's Ministry of Defence.

Despite having a dedicated top-level domain, the US military also uses _com_ domains for some of its recruitment sites, such as _goarmy.com_, as well as for the Defense Commissary Agency's website _www.commissaries.com_ and most non-appropriated fund instrumentalities such as military MWR organizations and military exchanges. Also, the military uses _edu_ domains for its service academies: the United States Military Academy, United States Coast Guard Academy, United States Naval Academy, and the United States Air Force Academy can all be reached using either an _edu_ or a _mil_ domain name. The official athletic program sites of the three academies that are members of NCAADivision I (Army, Navy, Air Force) use _com_ domains, as well as Coast Guard, which is a member of NCAA Division III. The United States Department of Defense (also referred to as the Department of War) itself uses _gov_ for its home page, with at least three second-level domains within _mil_ (_defense_, _dod_, _pentagon_) redirecting to its domain name war.govArchived September 5, 2025, at the Wayback Machine (formerly dod.gov).
The United States Coast Guard, like other military services, uses the _mil_ domain, although during statutory peacetime the service falls under the United States Department of Homeland Security.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/.mil#cite_note-2)
The _mil_ domain is also used by NORAD, a bi-national military alliance between the US and Canada.
1.   ↑Postel, J.; Reynolds, J. (October 1984). "RFC 920 - Domain Requirements". _The Internet Engineering Task Force_. doi:10.17487/RFC0920.  
2.   ↑"United States Coast Guard Regulations 1992"(PDF). US Coast Guard.

## What is the .MIL domain?
The .mil is one of the oldest generic top-level domains (gTLD) on the internet, created in 1985 alongside .com, .org, .net, .edu, and .gov, and administered ever since by the DoD Network Information Center (NIC), coordinated by the Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA), the agency that in practice manages the domain registry for the United States Department of Defense — officially renamed the Department of War in 2025.
Only second-level domain registration under .mil is permitted for US military services, unified or specified commands, and Department operating agencies that do not report through a specific military command chain; certain federal entities linked to the defense sector, though not strictly military, may also qualify in some cases. It is not available to the general public or to any organization outside the US defense structure. The application process requires providing verifiable evidence that the applicant is officially part of the armed forces, coordinating the process with DISA. A mandatory technical requirement: every second-level domain under .mil must have at least two nameservers, preferably hosted on two separate networks, to ensure service resilience.
**Registration restrictions**
Only second-level domain registration under .mil is permitted for US military services, unified or specified commands, and Department of Defense operating agencies that do not report through a specific military service chain. Applicants must provide verifiable evidence that they are an official part of the US armed forces, coordinating the process with DISA. At least two nameservers are required, preferably hosted on separate networks. Contact our team to confirm availability and the exact requirements.

The domain name **mil** is the sponsored top-level domain (sTLD) in the Domain Name System of the Internet for the United States Department of Defense and its subsidiary or affiliated organizations. The name is derived from _military_. It was one of the first top-level domains, created in January 1985.[[1]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/.mil?mobile-app=true&theme=wiki#cite_note-1)
The United States is the only country that has a top-level domain for its military, a legacy of the United States' military role in the creation of the Internet. Other countries often use second-level domains for this purpose, e.g., mod.uk for the United Kingdom's Ministry of Defence. Canada uses _norad.mil_ with the United States as they jointly operate the North American Aerospace Defense Command.
Although the United States military has its own top-level domain, it still uses com domains for some of its recruitment sites, such as _goarmy.com_, as well as for the Defense Commissary Agency's public website and most non-appropriated fund instrumentalities such as military MWR organizations and military exchanges. Also, the military uses edu domains for its service academies: the United States Military Academy, United States Coast Guard Academy, United States Naval Academy, and the United States Air Force Academy can all be reached using either an edu or a mil domain. The official athletic program sites of the three academies that are members of NCAA Division I (Army, Navy, Air Force) use com domains. The Department of Defense itself uses gov for its home page, with at least three second-level domains within mil ("defense", "dod", and "pentagon") redirecting to its home page of _defense.gov_.
The Department of Defense is also using vanity domain names within mil, such as ourmilitary.mil and norad.mil.
The United States Coast Guard uses the mil domain, despite the service being controlled by the United States Department of Homeland Security during statutory peacetime.

## References[]
1.   ↑RFC 920, _Domain Requirements_, J. Postel, J. Reynolds, The Internet Society (October 1984)

The United States is the only country that has a top-level domain for its military, a legacy of the United States' military role in the creation of the Internet. Other countries often use second-level domains for this purpose, e.g., mod.uk for the United Kingdom's Ministry of Defence. Canada uses _norad.mil_ with the United States as they jointly operate the North American Aerospace Defense Command.
Although the United States military has its own top-level domain, it still uses com domains for some of its recruitment sites, such as _goarmy.com_, as well as for the Defense Commissary Agency's public website and most non-appropriated fund instrumentalities such as military MWR organizations and military exchanges. Also, the military uses edu domains for its service academies: the United States Military Academy, United States Coast Guard Academy, United States Naval Academy, and the United States Air Force Academy can all be reached using either an edu or a mil domain. The official athletic program sites of the three academies that are members of NCAA Division I (Army, Navy, Air Force) use com domains. The Department of Defense itself uses gov for its home page, with at least three second-level domains within mil ("defense", "dod", and "pentagon") redirecting to its home page of _defense.gov_.
The Department of Defense is also using vanity domain names within mil, such as ourmilitary.mil and norad.mil.
The United States Coast Guard uses the mil domain, despite the service being controlled by the United States Department of Homeland Security during statutory peacetime.

The domain name **mil** is the sponsored top-level domain (sTLD) in the Domain Name System of the Internet for the United States Department of Defense and its subsidiary or affiliated organizations. The name is derived from _military_. It was one of the first top-level domains, created in January 1985.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/.mil#cite_note-1) As in the case with .gov, the United States is the only country that has a top-level domain for its military, a direct result of the United States' military's role in the creation of the Internet.
Other countries often use second-level domains for this purpose, e.g., _mod.uk_ for the United Kingdom's Ministry of Defence.

Despite having a dedicated top-level domain, the US military also uses _com_ domains for some of its recruitment sites, such as _goarmy.com_, as well as for the Defense Commissary Agency's website _www.commissaries.com_ and most non-appropriated fund instrumentalities such as military MWR organizations and military exchanges. Also, the military uses _edu_ domains for its service academies: the United States Military Academy, United States Coast Guard Academy, United States Naval Academy, and the United States Air Force Academy can all be reached using either an _edu_ or a _mil_ domain name. The official athletic program sites of the three academies that are members of NCAADivision I (Army, Navy, Air Force) use _com_ domains, as well as Coast Guard, which is a member of NCAA Division III. The United States Department of Defense (also referred to as the Department of War) itself uses _gov_ for its home page, with at least three second-level domains within _mil_ (_defense_, _dod_, _pentagon_) redirecting to its domain name war.govArchived September 5, 2025, at the Wayback Machine (formerly dod.gov).
The United States Coast Guard, like other military services, uses the _mil_ domain, although during statutory peacetime the service falls under the United States Department of Homeland Security.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/.mil#cite_note-2)
The _mil_ domain is also used by NORAD, a bi-national military alliance between the US and Canada.

## What is the .MIL domain?
The .mil is one of the oldest generic top-level domains (gTLD) on the internet, created in 1985 alongside .com, .org, .net, .edu, and .gov, and administered ever since by the DoD Network Information Center (NIC), coordinated by the Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA), the agency that in practice manages the domain registry for the United States Department of Defense — officially renamed the Department of War in 2025.
Only second-level domain registration under .mil is permitted for US military services, unified or specified commands, and Department operating agencies that do not report through a specific military command chain; certain federal entities linked to the defense sector, though not strictly military, may also qualify in some cases. It is not available to the general public or to any organization outside the US defense structure. The application process requires providing verifiable evidence that the applicant is officially part of the armed forces, coordinating the process with DISA. A mandatory technical requirement: every second-level domain under .mil must have at least two nameservers, preferably hosted on two separate networks, to ensure service resilience.
